Why We Still Print Things

By Grace Hopper

There is a particular kind of attention that only paper seems to summon. A printed page does not refresh, notify, autoplay or suggest. It just sits there, patiently, waiting to be read from the first line to the last. In an age of infinite scroll, that patience has become a feature rather than a limitation.

Researchers have long argued about whether reading on paper improves comprehension. The evidence is mixed, but one finding keeps returning: people who read long, complex texts on paper tend to remember the structure of an argument better. See the 2024 meta-study for details.

What makes a page print-friendly

Good print layouts share a handful of properties:

  • Generous margins and a comfortable measure of 60–75 characters.
  • Real typography: proper quotes, dashes, ligatures and hyphenation.
  • No navigation, no ads, and no "related stories" carousel.
    1. Especially no carousels.
    2. Really.

"The best interface is no interface." — someone who owned a printer

A tiny bit of code

Here is how you might count words in Rust, using split_whitespace:

fn word_count(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.split_whitespace().count() // #hash, *stars*, $dollars$
}

The numbers

MediumMinutes readRecall
Paper1872%
Screen1158%
Average65%

Special characters must survive the trip: 1. this is not a list, # nor a heading, = nor this, [brackets], _underscores_, back\slashes, @mentions, <angle brackets>, 50% off, AT&T, naïve café, Ελληνικά, 日本語, and emoji 📄.

In the end, printing an article is a small act of commitment. You decide that this, out of everything competing for your attention today, deserves a quiet half hour. That alone might be the best argument for paper.
